## Intent
Hypothesis: compiler auto-vectorization of the integration loop (LP1) alone can improve performance over naive scalar in an AoS layout, even with a simple branchy respawn loop (LP2) left unoptimized.

## Layout & approach
The AoS layout packs 68 B/particle across 11 fields, but each loop touches only a fraction: LP1 uses 24/68 B (35% hot — pos+vel), LP2 uses 8/68 B (11% hot — age+seed), and LP3 uses 28/68 B (41% hot — color+pos). The remaining 59–89% per loop is dead weight dragged through the line filler on every stride-68B access. No intermediate storage is allocated — the death verdict stays in registers — so all three loops walk the same 68-byte stride with no opportunity to compact the hot fields. The working set spills L1d at N≈481 and L2 at N≈7710, but because the hot fraction per loop is so small, effective capacity is far above the nominal transitions; the bottleneck is instruction/frontend pressure, not cache capacity.

## Cache saturation
The ns/p-vs-N curve is strikingly flat across all regimes. At q=0.01, cost rises only ~3 ns/p from L1d (21.9 ns/p at N=480) through L2 (25.1 at N=7700) into L3 (24.5–25.6 at N=10K–160K), with a modest DRAM knee at N=250000 (26.6 ns/p) settling near 29.2 at N=10M. The L1d→L2 and L2→L3 transitions are each sub-1-ns/p — nearly invisible. The DRAM transition adds ~2–3 ns/p but the curve flattens immediately after. Higher death rates shift the entire curve up (q=0.5: ~34–37 ns/p) without altering the shape. The dense grid resolves every transition, but none is the story: the flatness signals a non-cache bottleneck that dominates regardless of residency.

## Bandwidth
Achieved bandwidth spans 3.1 GB/s (N=480, q=0.01) down to 1.8 GB/s (N=1M, q=0.5) — only 14–24% of the 12.69 GB/s ceiling. The memory floor of 5.359 ns/p frames the irreducible memory time; this algo runs 4.1–7.0x above it, so memory is a minority of cost. The algo is frontend-bound: frontend stalls account for 64.2–74.5% of cycles across all profiles, compute only 14.4–35.4%, and backend stalls rise to 11–12% only in DRAM. Against the naive scalar baseline the algo is flat at 0.984–1.163x — the auto-vectorized LP1 buys nothing. Against the winner (AF02.LP1-autovec.LP2-opt) the gap is 1.96–3.6x, widest at low death rates (2.91x at q=0.01, N=480) and narrowest at q=0.5 (2.00x) where respawn pressure erodes the winner's optimized LP2 advantage.

## Assembly
Loop 1 is partially vectorized: `vmovups` loads the 16-byte pos chunk, `vshufps`/`vinsertps` rearrange components, and `vmulps`/`vaddps` execute the integration — 6 vector instructions among 21 total. Loops 2 and 3 are entirely scalar. Loop 2 (75 insns, 13 branches) uses `vucomiss`+`jae` for the death check, a `call` to spawn, and scalar RNG state manipulation (`rorx`, `lzcnt`, `xor`). Loop 3 (199 insns, 21 branches) is the heaviest: `vucomiss`+`vcvttss2si` convert floats to pixel coordinates, 12 `cmovae` implement clamping selects, and 16 byte-granular stores (`mov BYTE PTR`) scatter into the color buffer — each a read-modify-write on individual bytes. Only 15 of 367 instructions are vector-suffixed. The 64–75% frontend stall is explained by the 274 combined instructions of loops 2+3 with 34 conditional branches defeating the decoders.

## Verdict
Refuted — the algo runs at 0.984–1.163x of the naive scalar baseline at every N×q point, meaning the auto-vectorized LP1 provides no measurable benefit. It is 1.96–3.6x slower than the winner (AF02.LP1-autovec.LP2-opt) everywhere, with the gap widest at q=0.01 (2.91x at N=480) where the winner's optimized LP2 dominates and narrowest at q=0.5 (2.00x) where respawn pressure equalizes them. The mechanism: LP1's 6 vector instructions are drowned by loops 2+3's 274 scalar instructions with 34 branches, and the 64–75% frontend stall prevents the core from exploiting any cache locality the AoS layout might still offer.
